newsitem.title: UK: Baltic Exchange says to propose simpler membership.
newsitem.headline: Baltic Exchange says to propose simpler membership.

text.p: The Baltic Exchange said on Wednesday it will propose a radically simplified membership structure in the near future.

Baltic Exchange chief executive Jim Buckley told the dry cargo shipping market's annual general meeting: "A fresh proposal for a radically simplified membership structure will be made. We hope to be able to put it to members in the next few months."
Buckley said the new scheme would put the use of the Exchange's facilities on a corporate structure.
It would allow member firms to pay an all-in fee for the number of their staff using the Baltic rather than having to pay for separate memberships for each person attending the Exchange, he said.

However, the meeting did not address the controversial issue of putting a valuation on Baltic shares and a proposal to pay a special dividend of 100 sterling per share which was withdrawn before the AGM.

The membership proposal sits alongside plans the Baltic may put to members by the end of this year to rent out its private restaurant on the first floor and open a bar and dining facilities on its ground floor trading room.
Buckley said the Exchange had succeeded in reducing the Baltic's operating deficit which leaves it reliant on income from funds invested after the sale of its old site, bombed by the IRA.
However, the only way to dramatically cut the deficit was to earn an income on the 2,000 sq. ft first floor restaurant.
Buckley said interest had been shown in the restaurant and it could generate 100,000 stg a year in income.

At the same time the Baltic wanted to better utilise its 4,000 sq. ft trading floor which is only fully used on Mondays and for functions. Buckley put forward a plan to open a bar at one end with a sliding partition.

However, the Baltic would first experiment by throwing open the use of its facilities to all staff of member companies for a limited period in order to determine what theoretical demand there would be for them under the corporate membership scheme.
Chairman Eric Shawyer added: "Dividends will flow in the future. We will know better by the end of the year if we can get more people to use the facilities."
The Baltic today paid its traditional one pound dividend per share and also amended its rules to allow foreign persons and companies to become members.
